title: Examining the Chiefs’ short-yardage offense through four weeks
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs are enjoying an early-season bye week, sitting at a perfect 4-0 record. The only undefeated team left in the AFC, the Chiefs have one of the best offenses in the NFL and are currently third in the league with 1,648 yards of total offense. Running back Kenneth Walker has breathed new […]
full_text: (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs are enjoying an early-season bye week, sitting at a perfect 4-0 record. The only undefeated team left in the AFC, the Chiefs have one of the best offenses in the NFL and are currently third in the league with 1,648 yards of total offense. Running back Kenneth Walker has breathed new life into the Chiefs’ offense and has led the NFL in rushing so far with 537 yards through the four-game stretch. Walker has helped the Chiefs offense in dozens of ways, but even with his ability, the Chiefs have still been inconsistent in short-yardage situations this season. At times, third-and-fourth-and-short conversions have been automatic, but in recent weeks the Chiefs have struggled to convert. Let’s dive into what works and what the team needs to improve on. A look at the numbers The offense ranks 10th in the league in 4th-down conversion percentage at 62.5%, while ranking 12th in red-zone touchdown rate at 63.16%. As many remember, the Chiefs led the league in 4th-down conversion percentage last year at a whopping 75%, thanks largely to Kareem Hunt’s dominant short-yardage season. The Chiefs weren’t quite as good in the red zone, but they still finished 12th in the league with a 56.3% touchdown conversion rate once they entered the red zone. The season is only a quarter old, but this appears to be an area where the Chiefs may have regressed early in the season in short-yardage-to-go situations. A look at the tape shows that a few tweaks could help the Chiefs improve as the season progresses. What’s worked On opening night, the Chiefs wasted no time rolling out a “jumbo” package on the first 4th-and-short. Motion creates a full house look with Tonga in the FB slot. Not a tremendous amount of movement up front, but Walker slips the DT and gets a good seal from Humphrey to pickup the first on 4th down. pic.twitter.com/Kz4Wqa2Vb9 — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) September 15, 2026 Out of a full house set with an overloaded offensive line, the Chiefs needed only a yard. With nose tackle Khyiris Tonga lined up at fullback, the Chiefs go with their version of a dive play up the middle. Only needing a yard, Walker uses good vision to find an opening and slip through for three yards and a first down. On the next fourth-and-short, the Broncos would try to take away the middle, but the Chiefs had a bigger play in mind. Big runs don't just happen. It is the culmination of many little things and all the things that make football great. KC runs power on 4th down, and Denver pinches. Why pinch? When was the last time a Chiefs RB bounced on a 4th and short? Walker reads it immediately and is gone. pic.twitter.com/0VGsUcD8mZ — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) September 15, 2026 The defense tries to pinch to take away the middle, but the Chiefs run power to the left and catch the Broncos slanting inside, with safeties crashing in. The play isn’t well blocked, but Tonga gets just enough to buy Walker time to get outside and break it to the house. A week later, the Chiefs would show a few wrinkles in short yardage to keep defenses guessing. When KC wants to convert with Tonga, it is paramount that he builds momentum and gets into a position to create a second wave of momentum behind the OL. pic.twitter.com/AAvjJ38Kfj — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) October 10, 2026 To keep defenses respecting Tonga, the Chiefs have given him the ball a few times this season, and in Week 2 against the Indianapolis Colts , it worked perfectly when he blasted ahead and rode the offensive line’s momentum for a first down. Later in the game, with the defense keyed in on Walker and Tonga, the Chiefs executed a beautiful play-action look in the low red zone. Out of the jumbo look, having WR's line up in line is a great way to free up players in space. With all eyes on Walker and Tonga, Mahomes makes a great run sell and delivers it to Royals in the back of the endzone. pic.twitter.com/EV5OfVf54n — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) October 10, 2026 Out of the jumbo look with Tonga as the fullback in an I-formation, the Chiefs go with a play-action look. Jalen Royals lines up as a Y, as the Chiefs have shown on prior looks, but on the snap, he releases and is wide open in the end zone. In the first couple of weeks of the season, the Chiefs’ short-yardage attack looked unstoppable, but in the last couple of weeks, it has struggled. Issues In Weeks 3 and 4, the Chiefs struggled to convert on fourth and short, and the issues started up front. 4th and 1 KC tries to go power, but the down blocks give up too much penetration, and the puller doesn't stay tight enough on the LOS. pic.twitter.com/LqFNFTIFCX — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) October 10, 2026 On fourth down, the Chiefs go with their jumbo set with Walker as the single back. On the snap, they run power, and Walker tries to cut inside quickly, but he is stuffed and falls short of the first down. The defense penetrates through the down side of the offensive line, and Kansas City’s front creates little push. Walker had to make a quick decision and tried to cut it up the middle, but he could not get through. Last week against the Las Vegas Raiders , the Chiefs still struggled to convert on fourth down, and once again the defense penetrated the front to stuff Walker. KC is going zone here, with Tonga and Gray lead blocking, but the penetration in the B gap plugs the way and allows the second-level players to flow down quickly and stop Walker's momentum. pic.twitter.com/bwODfcM0QK — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) October 10, 2026 The Chiefs go with zone out of the full-house set and a jumbo offensive line. Once again, penetration through the B-gap causes a hold-up and stops momentum. Walker tries to navigate around it, but the Raiders linebackers fill quickly and close the hole to stop him before he can break free. The bottom line The Chiefs have all the talent to convert fourth down at will, so the issues over the last two weeks have been concerning, especially since they showed what they are capable of in the first two weeks of the season. Converting on fourth and short is about creating a charge at the line and having the ball carrier make a quick decision off it. Penetration from the defensive front ruins looks and can change the game’s outcome. So far, these issues haven’t affected the Chiefs’ win-and-loss record, but they must improve in this area moving forward. The talent and play calls are there; the team must simply execute in these critical moments.

title: Looking at advanced stats behind the Chiefs’ hot start
summary: With the Kansas City Chiefs enjoying an early bye in Week 5, it is a great time to look at trends from the first half of the season. As one of the league’s three remaining undefeated teams, it is unsurprising that many metrics favor what Kansas City has done over the first four weeks. Let’s […]
full_text: (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images With the Kansas City Chiefs enjoying an early bye in Week 5, it is a great time to look at trends from the first half of the season. As one of the league’s three remaining undefeated teams, it is unsurprising that many metrics favor what Kansas City has done over the first four weeks. Let’s take a look at some interesting tidbits from the NFL’s Next Gen Stats on Chiefs’ strong start — and what areas of concern remain. Offense The biggest factor in Kansas City’s early success has been a true commitment to the run game that few expected head coach Andy Reid to be capable of. Right now, Kansas City ranks second in expected points added (EPA) per run play at 0.14. The only team ahead is the Buffalo Bills , who benefit in the metric from quarterback Josh Allen’s ability to make plays with his legs. Speedy Buffalo running back James Cook also narrowly edges Walker (at 15 to 14) on rush attempts of ten or more yards. Walker leads all running backs with 10.9 cumulative expected points added. His 537 total yards easily lead the league. In fact, his four-game total will likely only fall to second in the league — even after most teams have a five-game sample. Bijan Robinson of the Atlanta Falcons trails Walker by 43 yards and probably will pass him even with a below-average performance. Cook could push Walker to third place in the NFL’s rushing leaders with 117 yards on the ground when the Bills face the Los Angeles Rams on Monday night. By many metrics, quarterback Patrick Mahomes is having his best season since winning his second MVP award in 2022. His EPA per dropback currently stands at 0.17, up from 0.11 each of the past two seasons. There has been no noticeable uptick in the face of the league testing his deep ball (unsurprising given the continuing questions at offensive tackle. Mahomes’ 7.1 air yards per attempt is up from the 2023 and 2024 seasons, but it’s a slight decline from his 7.9-yard mark in his truncated 2025 campaign. The Chiefs are currently running about 40% of their offensive plays from under center (up from about 18% in 2025). Walker’s addition is also allowing Mahomes to reach a career-high 33% play-action percentage on passing plays. The only other time Mahomes exceeded 30% as a starter was in 2018, when he played most of the season with second-year running back Kareem Hunt. One curiosity of the start is the usage of rookie running back Emmett Johnson. With only five receptions (on five targets), Johnson already has a cumulative 5.8 receiving EPA. Because of a -3.6-yard average depth of target, Johnson has been credited with 92 yards after the catch while officially having 74 receiving yards for the year. Reid and his staff should prioritize unlocking Johnson’s potential in the screen game in the weeks ahead. Defense In recent weeks, the Chiefs’ defense has reminded many fans of the importance of taking prescribed blood pressure medication. However, most advanced stats spin what the unit is doing in a favorable light. Kansas City’s -.010 EPA per defensive play ranks eighth in the league through the season’s first month. When separated into run and pass plays, the Chiefs remain in the top ten in both. The run defense has been particularly effective when using light boxes. The Chiefs rank second with a -0.27 EPA when having fewer than seven players near the line. Surprisingly, Kansas City’s stuff rate (plays stopped behind the line of scrimmage or for no gain) sits at about 21% in any box formation. Overall, the 21.2% stuff rate ranks third in the league. The Chiefs have been much more susceptible to run plays on third down, however. In the key situation, Kansas City’s EPA drops to 0.28, good for 21st overall. Passing stats on third down trend more toward league average. Veteran cornerback L’Jarius Sneed is widely seen as a liability to the defense, and advanced metrics mostly agree. Sneed has allowed 278 receiving yards in coverage, the fourth most in the league. He also has been targeted on 30% of the coverage snaps he has taken. With a -6.2 pass coverage EPA, linebacker Drue Tranquill narrowly misses a spot in the NFL’s top ten. We will be back with another look at how advanced metrics view the Chiefs as they enter a ‘mini bye’ after their Thanksgiving night game against the Bills.

title: The Rams should call up Brennan Presley to return punts
summary: What if the Los Angeles Rams had a player with a long history of both punt and kickoff returns, that at the risk of being over dramatic, is just languishing on the practice squad? Brennan Presley is on the Rams’ practice squad and he could be the answer to rekindle some explosivity to their return […]
full_text: What if the Los Angeles Rams had a player with a long history of both punt and kickoff returns, that at the risk of being over dramatic, is just languishing on the practice squad? Brennan Presley is on the Rams’ practice squad and he could be the answer to rekindle some explosivity to their return game if they call him up. It is only Week 5 and the L.A. special teams unit is already in disarray. It’s not a new topic, it feels like a year-to-year discussion since Sean McVay parted ways with John Fassell after the 2019 season. Fans have been weighing in on the current regime since early spring and TST has had plenty to say about it. The Rams coverage units are 30th in punt return average allowed (14.4) and 22nd in kickoffs (27.0). Return units rank 18th for punts (9.0) and 31st in kickoffs (21.9). While the Rams have made a concerted effort to shore up leaky coverage with outside players, they don’t appear to have done the same due diligence in the return game. Brennan Presley will go down as an Oklahoma State legend. In his time in Stillwater @bprezzle proved he could do it all and showed he had the heart of a warrior. He leaves Stillwater as the all time receptions leader and amassed 315 rec 3,315 yards 23 Tds 30 rushes 160 yards 6… pic.twitter.com/CEAq2xam3i — Dustin J (@405pokefan) December 11, 2024 Signed by the Rams in 2025, out of the undrafted ranks. 24 years old and diminutive in stature, 5’ 8” 175 lb. Left Oklahoma State at or towards the top of their all-time receiving, all-purpose and return lists Since he didn’t get into a regular season game in 2025, to grade and project Presley, fans have to go by his work and numbers from college days at Oklahoma State. He started in 44 of 63 games played and left as OSU’s all-time leader in pass receptions and towards the top in all receiving categories, chalking up 315 catches for 3315 yards and 23 scores. To compliment those receiving yards, he averaged over 1000 yards per season in all-purpose production, chipping in 160 yards rushing, 1427 in kickoff return yardage, and 240 yards on punt returns. Presley posted strong athletic testing numbers at the Big 12 Pro Day. To go along with very good long speed (4.46) he showed plus burst, balance, flexibility, change of direction (6.71 shuttle) and short-area agility (4.07 3cone) to go along with very good long speed. His ability to run with the ball stands out. A jitterbug style with slippery-fast change of direction and makes his cuts at speed. If given sliver of space, he seems to always beat the first tackler, played running back in high school and runs with willing physicality for a small player. Presley is not what I would grade as a “can’t miss” returner, but does bring the right skillset and background. His darting open-field style hasn’t been seen a pro game, but he’s looked solid in preseason work. Because of his ability with ball in his hands, he does double duty as a receiver and his traits carry over to both. Oklahoma State flooded him with a lot of short/mid range routes to utilize that advantage. He was predominantly a slot receiver, but also saw reps outside, in bunch sets, and in motion. He came to L.A. needing to expand his route tree, but showed off good hands, ball tracking, and body control to reel in imperfect passes. Like most small receivers, he’ll need to adjust physical press coverage and could have issues at the catch point against bigger, longer secondary players. He does have a good feel for soft areas in zones and works back to his quarterback when flushed from the pocket. At a very good price, Presley can wear a lot of hats as a versatile special teams piece piece to go along with work on offense. In fact, during his first three college seasons, he not only worked as a returner, but played on coverage units as a gunner as well. He was lauded by coaches for his work ethic, leadership and competitive juices. Ty Simpson to Brennan Presley for the TOUCHDOWN‼️ pic.twitter.com/vzIexlolbg — Ethan Shirazi (@Ethanshirazi24) August 28, 2026 Are the Rams ready/willing to make this decision? Probably not. Just a week ago, we fans found out how much weight should be given to what L.A. special teams coordinator Bubba Ventrone offers on the unit’s progress, or lack thereof.. In a 10/1 Thursday presser, Ventrone gave Xavier Smith, the Rams primary punt returner for three seasons, his public support and 24 hours later, the XMan was jettisoned. While very few fans would disagree with the move, how the Rams handled it does cause some raised eyebrows. Sean McVay wasted no time in naming Alex Bachman as the new returner, deep on both kickoffs and punts. In all fairness, grading Bachman on one game is a tiny sample, but the film of the Eagle game left a lot to be desired. After nine seasons, his only playing in 24 total games, with 27 punt returns (22 last year) and eight kickoff returns doesn’t inspire much confidence. Last Sunday, I offered six candidates for the Rams return game and said this about the Rans decision to install Bachman as of now, the primary kick returner, “…I have to wonder how many would consider this move an upgrade. Although Bachman fielded a fair amount of kicks for the Las Vegas Raiders last year, he does not have a history as a returner., nor is he known as an open-field runner. His production was only mediocre It appears a lateral move, at best.” The Rams need to see what they’ve got with Brennan Presley. The status quo is not making anything better.

title: Rams vs Bills: How to watch on TV, stream, or listen on radio
summary: After two weeks on the road, the Los Angeles Rams get back home to SoFi Stadium for an October 12 matchup with the Buffalo Bills. The Monday Night Football kickoff is set for 5:15 p.m. PDT. Back onto even ground at 2-2, L.A. will try to get on the plus side of the ledger against […]
full_text: The Rams defense needs to corral Buffalo Bills QB Josh Allen (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images) | Getty Images After two weeks on the road, the Los Angeles Rams get back home to SoFi Stadium for an October 12 matchup with the Buffalo Bills. The Monday Night Football kickoff is set for 5:15 p.m. PDT. Back onto even ground at 2-2, L.A. will try to get on the plus side of the ledger against a 3-1 Bills team whose only blemish came in last Sunday’s fourth quarter loss to the New England Patriots. Limiting the Buffalo run game and forcing them into a one-dimensional offense would pay dividends for the Rams. James Cook has pretty much been a one-man band for the Bills rush attack, while he’s not a power back, his vision and one-cut style make him a solid fit into Buffalo’s outside zone-based run game. He’s possesses the open-field moves and speed to gash defenses. Although quarterback Josh Allen hasn’t accrued a lot of yards in 2026, he’s still quite dangerous extending plays by breaking from the pocket or on designed runs. His size and athleticism creates big problems down near the goal line. Already this year, he’s got seven touchdowns on the ground. The Rams lead the all-time series by a 9-6 margin, a limited Rams/Bills history. Although Buffalo was a founding member of the American Football league, there was no inter-league play until the 1970 NFL/AFL merger. Since Sean McVay took charge of the Rams in 2017, the two squads have met three times and Buffalo holds a 2-1 advantage. Here’s how to follow the game! Location: SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, Ca. title: Nate Landman fined by NFL for a second time this season
summary: The NFL fined L.A. Rams linebacker Nate Landman $11,111 for a hit on a defenseless player this week. The penalty came in the second quarter of the Rams’ Week 4 win over the Philadelphia Eagles, as Landman was flagged for a hit on receiver Dontayvion Wicks. The Eagles ended up punting a few plays later. […]
full_text: The NFL fined L.A. Rams linebacker Nate Landman $11,111 for a hit on a defenseless player this week. The penalty came in the second quarter of the Rams’ Week 4 win over the Philadelphia Eagles, as Landman was flagged for a hit on receiver Dontayvion Wicks. The Eagles ended up punting a few plays later. Landman was previously fined $11,111 for an unnecessary roughness “use of the helmet” penalty against the San Francisco 49ers in Week 1. The NFL fined a season-high 10 players for "major" fouls in Week 4: 🏈 Ravens LB Trenton Simpson ($17,911 for horse collar tackle) 🏈 Browns DT Adin Huntington ($5,620 for hip-drop tackle) 🏈 Cowboys CB Reddy Steward ($5,583 for hit on defenseless player) 🏈 Broncos OL Ben… — Tom Pelissero (@TomPelissero) October 10, 2026 It’s already the third significant roughness penalty against Landman in his last seven games, dating back to the 2025 playoffs and the Carolina Panthers. Landman previously avoided a fine in the 2026 playoffs for this hit on Panthers receiver Jalen Coker. Nate Landman hit. Jalen Coker was in bounds, and got hit sticked by Nate Landman. WOW BRO 🤯 pic.twitter.com/C4W7lkUM8l — SM Highlights (@SMHighlights1) January 11, 2026 The Rams signed Eric Kendricks this week , perhaps as insurance for the linebacker position moving forward. Landman signed a three-year, $22 million extension with L.A. in 2025, but he hasn’t been as impactful since that deal and it’s starting to make more sense why the Atlanta Falcons let him walk after only three seasons with his original team. Landman mainly just tackles players and that’s about it. Sometimes the tackles are loud and powerful and possibly painful, which is all within the bounds of football. Sometimes they deliver free first downs and get him fined, so that’s something he will need to clean up moving forward.

title: Browns player says Jared Verse is a better leader than Myles Garrett
summary: When the Los Angeles Rams pushed in their chips for Myles Garrett, many said the greatest cost was not draft picks going to the Cleveland Browns, but it was giving up pass rusher Jared Verse. Although Verse leaves a lot to be desired in production — he has zero sacks in his first four games […]
full_text: When the Los Angeles Rams pushed in their chips for Myles Garrett, many said the greatest cost was not draft picks going to the Cleveland Browns, but it was giving up pass rusher Jared Verse. Although Verse leaves a lot to be desired in production — he has zero sacks in his first four games with the Browns — cornerback Denzel Ward told the PFF NFL Show that he is more of a “vocal leader” than Garrett . “Definitely brought a lot of juice and just mentality, as well,” Ward said on the “PFF NFL Show” of what Verse brings. “Myles is a heck of a player, great player, but I think Jared, he’s more vocal, more of a vocal player, vocal leader out there for us. Since the first day he stepped in the building, just yelling, screaming and making his mark out there in meetings and on the practice field, kind of rallying guys. So definitely respect who he is as a player and the way he approaches the game and how he brings guys along.” This is actually not that surprising, nor does it change the fact that Verse is still miles behind Garrett as an actual football player. Jared Verse is not good at finishing plays Through 38 career games, Verse has 12 sacks. In his first 10 games last season, Garrett had 15 sacks . Verse has zero sacks through four games this season and now instead of the Rams making excuses for him, it’s Browns defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg . “When you look at games, everybody is looking for the ‘ooh’ and the ‘wow’ play,” Rutenberg said. “That’s not what defense is. Defense is about violence, chaos, disruption, and getting the ball. And it’s 11 dudes hunting on defense, and he’s hunting on defense, and somebody might ‘ooh’ and ‘ah’, great pick, but go watch the tape. Jared Verse might be disrupting the quarterback on that play. I’m going to go back to the Tampa Bay game where he chased it down from the backside. “That’s what defense is about. It’s creating chaos and disruption, and he’s doing that.” Though Verse has always been good at creating pressures, he’s one of the worst in the NFL at turning those pressures into sacks. Per Next Gen Stats, Verse has the second-lowest rate of converting pressures to sacks (7.9%) of any edge rusher in the NFL since 2024. He has nine pressures this season with zero sacks. So no matter what Rutenberg or anyone else says about him, teams don’t lose their minds over pass rushers who don’t finish plays. I’ve always put it this way: A sack is a sack, so it’s always a negative play for the offense. A pressure could result in anything. It could be a touchdown pass. Then there’s the question of whether or not Verse is even a good pass rusher at all. Per DMAC Football Analytics, Verse has a pressure rate of 12% on true pass sets and he’s probably less valuable than some of his Browns teammates. Verse has 20 pass rush snaps against the Steelers in Week 4 and generated zero pressures. He also went 0/16 against the Jaguars in Week 1. Jared Verse is only generating a 12% pressure rate on true pass sets. Verse only had 10.0% of the team's pressures on TPS despite having 15.7% of the pass rush attempts, for a -6.4% PSOE (pressure share over expected) which is 76th/84 EDGE rushers with >8% pass rush share on TPS. https://t.co/qAPAGGdw08 — DMAC Football Analytics (@DMACAnalytics) October 9, 2026 Virtually all of his pressures came against the Panthers in Week 3. Verse has a 9% pressure rate on 100 pass rushes this season, whereas teammate Maliek Collins has a 9.4% rate on 106. Verse is producing fewer pressures per play than Maliek Collins. He has a lower pressure rate than Isaiah McGuire, a 2023 fourth round pick who has a pressure rate of 12.9% on 93 attempts. And McGuire has two sacks. Mason Graham, Cleveland’s top pick in 2025, has four sacks already. He’s playing like an elite defensive lineman. Veteran Derek Barnett has a pressure rate of 17.9% on the same defense. So on one hand we’re always being told, “Don’t look at sacks with Jared, look at pressures.” But on the other hand, if we compare him to Barnett, people say “Don’t look at pressure rate, watch the tape.” Well guess what: Nobody ever traded Jared Verse and three draft picks, including a first, for a player with 7 sacks. They only offer that kind of package for someone like Myles Garrett because he leads the league in sacks. Myles Garrett may not be playing right now, but he has the same number of sacks as Jared Verse. This trade has been a disaster for the Rams. https://t.co/VdXC1OzpJQ — Grant Cohn (@grantcohn) October 9, 2026 Garrett never considered a leader Ward’s comments about Garrett are not surprising because we heard rumblings of Garrett’s quiet demeanor and off-brand style of leadership over the summer after he was traded to L.A . However, when I hear that Verse is really vocal in Cleveland I have to wonder if any players are secretly rolling their eyes. Denzel Ward is 29 and he’s been in the NFL for nine seasons. Does he really need a 25-year-old with zero sacks to speak up in order for the team to be motivated? Would you trade a loud edge rusher with zero sacks for a quiet player with 15? Of course, Myles Garrett does have to show up and play for the Rams eventually. Until that happens, it’s hard to declare L.A. the winners of the trade, or even just satisfied. But when I look over at the “centerpiece’ who went to Cleveland in the deal, I still don’t see a player who has significantly moved the needle at any point in his career. Getting pressures is not what tilts the field as a pass rusher. The great ones get the ball. Verse told reporters this week that he still hasn’t taken “the meal out of the microwave yet” in terms of his potential as a pass rusher in the NFL: Jared Verse used the time off to evaluate himself and what he can still bring to #Browns defense “I don’t even think I took the meal out of the microwave yet” pic.twitter.com/tVY4nXskj2 — Daryl Ruiter (@RuiterWrongFAN) October 8, 2026 Well…When are you planning to do that Jared? Jared Verse is not young. Not for a third-year player. He turns 26 next month. When Garrett was 26, he had 58.5 sacks and two first team All-Pro nods. In his age-26 season, Garrett had 16 sacks. Verse still needs four sacks just to get to 16 for his career. The Rams traded Verse for Garrett and they may have been reluctant to do so, but I also think they were hyping him up in the media after the deal because they had to hype him up in their trade talks with Cleveland . In reality, L.A. probably knew that Jared Verse has done more than scratch the surface. He’s always been talking about getting better in the future, but the NFL is about the present. And even though Garrett is injured and may not be the most vocal player when he’s healthy, we should all know what matters on the field: Speaking with actions, not words.

title: Sean McVay should never give up playcalling
summary: Sean Payton and DeMeco Ryans spent the last few days unwinding the exact decision that Sean McVay has refused to make. The head coaches of the Denver Broncos and Houston Texans took playcalling duties back from their coordinators after early-season struggles. The lesson for the Los Angeles Rams is simple: don’t create an unnecessary problem […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 4: Head coach Sean McVay of the Los Angeles Rams reacts after a touchdown in the fourth quarter against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on October 4, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The Rams defeated the Eagles 24-20. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Sean Payton and DeMeco Ryans spent the last few days unwinding the exact decision that Sean McVay has refused to make. The head coaches of the Denver Broncos and Houston Texans took playcalling duties back from their coordinators after early-season struggles. The lesson for the Los Angeles Rams is simple: don’t create an unnecessary problem you then must fix in October. Payton handed the Broncos’ offensive keys to Davis Webb in an effort to retain the rising star on the coaching staff. Denver is now 2-2 after making the AFC Championship game last season. Quarterback Bo Nix has just five touchdowns and three interceptions. On Thursday Payton said, “ We’ll make a change offensively; I’ll call the plays. ” He framed it as instincts and experience. Webb, who last offseason was on the cusp of the head coaching ranks, is now directionless. In Houston, Ryans took defensive playcalling back from Matt Burke following a winless start after four weeks. The Texans were one of the NFL’s best defenses over the last two years. So far they look nothing like themselves. Communication lapses and production worse than their talent level are the main culprits. Burke actually took playcalling responsibilities from Ryans last year after a similar 0-3 start. This year the script has flipped. But does it really matter which man pulls the strings? Teams cannot change schemes overnight. The selection might vary, but the menu is largely still the same. Even if head coaches are not the primary playcaller, they still provide significant input throughout the game. It’s likely a role that garners far more media coverage than it deserves. NFL franchises are not coaching factories. Would it be a positive for the Broncos or Texans if their hot shot coordinators eventually join the head coaching ranks? Of course. Bad teams rarely see their coaches leave for promotions. Greener pastures also help recruit new talent. The Rams don’t pay Sean McVay around $15M annually because he is adept at developing coaches for other teams. They fork over the big bucks because he gives his offense an edge through his scheme and calling the right plays at the right time. Handing over the duties to Nate Scheelhaase because he’s on the head coaching radar would be silly, even if Scheelhaase leaving would net the team two future third-round picks. Payton and Ryans are admitting—very publicly—that the title of head coach does not require surrendering the thing you’re best at. Payton has been a playcaller for the better part of two decades. Ryans built his reputation as a defensive mind. They tried to outsource the job, watched the product suffer, and reclaimed it. That is not emulation. It’s damage control. No one wants to see an emulation of McVay calling plays. We deserve the real thing. And we will probably get it for a while longer. Sean McVay shouldn’t and likely won’t give up playcalling after watching the very public and recent discourse surrounding Sean Payton and DeMeco Ryans.

title: What do you think of Matthew Stafford’s start to 2026?
summary: Matthew Stafford has thrown 6 interceptions in four games with over 1,100 passing yards (21 rushing yards) and six touchdowns. You can debate how Stafford’s start to the season has been because the six interceptions aren’t ideal, but the other stats are pretty good. So, how you think his start to 2026 has been? Stafford […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - OCTOBER 04: Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford #9 looks on during the game between the Los Angeles Rams and the Philadelphia Eagles on October 4, 2026 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA.(Photo by Andy Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Matthew Stafford has thrown 6 interceptions in four games with over 1,100 passing yards (21 rushing yards) and six touchdowns . You can debate how Stafford’s start to the season has been because the six interceptions aren’t ideal, but the other stats are pretty good. So, how you think his start to 2026 has been? Stafford can still sling it. Below is an attention-grabbing idea of “ Father Time catching up with Stafford” , and four games in it doesn’t quite look like that. It does look like Stafford may not match his MVP level of play in 2025. Then again, you could argue if Stafford can cut the picks, keep up and or increase the production, then he could regain that type of MVP form. The odds of Stafford winning back-to-back MVP’s are incredibly unlikely so we aren’t saying that. Still, so far, he has shown the arm to deliver that type of high caliber performances and moments. It’s been a bit of a polarizing start to the season for Stafford and the Rams, and with a 2-2 record, polarizing making plenty of sense as the description of the team to this point. They play their best at times; they play their worst at times. They’re polarizing. Stafford’s play has been a part of that. ‘Has Father Time Caught Up With You?’ — NFL Analyst Puts Matthew Stafford on Notice After Reigning MVP’s Worrying Start To Season (sports.yahoo) “Chris Broussard Questions Whether Matthew Stafford Is Showing His Age During “First Things First,” Broussard challenged Stafford to show that his best football remains available on a consistent basis. “Matthew Stafford, has father time caught up with you? I think that’s a legitimate question at this point,” Broussard said . He acknowledged that Stafford still delivers impressive moments. His concern was how much those flashes actually reveal about the quarterback’s overall level of play. “At times, you still look great, but that’s what happens. Even old guys can look great at times,” Broussard continued. Broussard pointed to Stafford’s six interceptions through four games, including four over his previous two appearances. He then delivered the challenge behind his assessment. “So, you have to go out there and prove that you are still that guy,” Broussard said .“ Matthew Stafford evaluates his performance in Rams’ first 4 games (ramswire) Matthew Stafford took home his first MVP award last season after throwing for a league-high 4,707 yards and 46 touchdowns. His numbers to start this year have paled in comparison, only tossing six touchdown passes and six interceptions in four games. Suffice to say, it’s been an up-and-down season thus far, mixing big-time throws with costly mistakes that have led to turnovers and points for the other team. Now that the first quarter of the season is in the books, Stafford evaluated his play when asked during Thursday’s press conference. He admitted he can certainly be better and wishes he had some throws back. “Definitely room for improvement,” he said. “There have been some really bright moments and some stuff I’m really proud of and stuff that I definitely wish I could take back to help us be in a better position to win games. That comes with the position. I understand that. I’ve been doing it a long time. I want to do everything I can to put our team in the best position to succeed. I’ve done that sometimes this year and other times I have not. I want to make sure that I do that at a more consistent clip moving forward.” Matthew Stafford Isn’t Hiding From His Turnovers, and the Rams Need It to Show Against Buffalo (athlonsports) “The Rams are 2-2 with an offense that ranks second in total yards and 19th in scoring. Eight giveaways have a lot to do with that gap. PFF has charged Stafford with eight turnover-worthy plays , which ranks 28th among quarterbacks, and his 65.4 grade sits 22nd of 34. Sumer Sports lists the Rams with the league’s fourth-highest interception rate at 3.64%. He threw a pick-six in Denver during a 30-26 loss, then two more interceptions in the first half against the Eagles before the 24-20 comeback.“ Fantasy football Week 5 Start ‘Em & Sit ‘Em: Matthew Stafford gets right back on track vs. Bills (cbssports) “It’s been a rocky start to the season so far for Stafford, but he should have a dominant game in Week 5 against Buffalo. I like Stafford as a top-three Fantasy quarterback in all leagues. He has two games this year with at least 24.9 Fantasy points and two others with 9.7 Fantasy points or less. Puka Nacua missed two games with a groin injury, but he’s healthy now. And Stafford is throwing the ball a lot with at least 51 pass attempts in his past two outings against Denver and Philadelphia. He’s only played one game at home this season (Week 2 against the Giants), and Stafford scored 34.9 Fantasy points. This week, we could get a shootout against the Bills, who are No. 5 in most Fantasy points allowed to opposing quarterbacks. C.J. Stroud, Jared Goff and Drake Maye each scored at least 20.5 Fantasy points against Buffalo, with Goff and Maye going over 32 Fantasy points. That’s the expectation I have for Stafford, who should be in a potential shootout with Josh Allen since this game has a projected total score of 53.5 points. I’m excited to see how good Stafford can be in Week 5, and he should have one of his best games of the season against Buffalo at home.” All eyes on SoFi Stadium as the Rams & the Bills battle on MNF | Game Preview (therams.com) “If you love tight end play, this is the game for you. According to NFL Pro, the Bills have used multiple tight ends on more than half their plays this season, buying into the Rams-led league-wide trend. However, with Colby Parkinson and Terrance Ferguson injured last week, the Rams used 13 personnel on just one snap, their fewest in a full calendar year. Fortunately, Parkinson is trending in the right direction to return, and it doesn’t sound like Ferguson should miss more than the required four weeks on injured reserve. In the meantime, Tyler Higbee has found the fountain of youth. I’m not sure Kyren Williams has put together better consecutive games than his performances in Denver and Philadelphia. Kudos to his scheme, offensive line, and LA’s all-11 approach to getting removal in the run game.“ Rams must keep Josh Allen uncomfortable as he seeks get-right game in LA (ramblinfan) “In a Week 3 win against the Chargers, he threw two picks versus no touchdowns and posted a passer rating of 54.0. For once, Allen was definitely not the reason Buffalo won. For the Rams, keeping him out of sync early will be key to LA’s chances. If Allen settles into a rhythm, the only path to victory will be in a shootout. Rams must get after Josh Allen out of the gate Overall, the Rams’ pass rush has underwhelmed this season, due in part because Myles Garrett has played all of one injury-hampered game. Although eligible to return off injured reserve at any time, His return date remains TBD. Aaron Donald missed last game with back soreness but the team is hopeful that he will play in Week 5.“ Buffalo Bills at Los Angeles Rams | Where to watch, stream and listen | MNF Week 5 (buffalobills.com) “The Bills look to bounce back after their first loss of the season in Week 4 on primetime against the Rams. Buffalo hits the road for the first time in three weeks, taking on a Los Angeles squad filled with star talent.” Rams’ Aaron Donald ready to return against the Bills (ocregister) ““I feel good, I feel good,” Donald said. “I feel a lot better than what I was.” Donald came out of the Rams’ Week 3 loss to the Broncos with a sore back. He was unable to practice last week and was held out of the Rams’ win over the Eagles . It was a decision that…

full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Las Vegas Raiders’ starting running back Ashton Jeanty is active for Sunday’s game at the New England Patriots. Jeanty, the No. 6 overall pick in the 2025 NFL draft, apparently injured his foot in practice Thursday and he did not practice Friday as the team prepared to play at the New England Patriots on Sunday. title: How Raiders can pull off Week 5 win
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders are sitting at 3-1 and looking to rebound from a 30-27 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs. A trip to Foxboro, Massachusetts, and the first 10:00 a.m. West Coast time game is up next. The New England Patriots and head coach Mike Vrabel are a good team, but they aren’t unbeatable. […]
full_text: (Photo by Barry Chin/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) The Las Vegas Raiders are sitting at 3-1 and looking to rebound from a 30-27 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs. A trip to Foxboro, Massachusetts, and the first 10:00 a.m. West Coast time game is up next. The New England Patriots and head coach Mike Vrabel are a good team, but they aren’t unbeatable. If the Raiders do these five things, they can get back to their winning ways. 1. Pressuring Drake Maye Maye had a get-right game against their division rival, the Buffalo Bills, last week. Throwing for 269 yards and three touchdowns, plus leading his team in rushing with 54 yards. How was he able to do this? As a whole, the Bills’ defense only produced five quarterback hits and one sack. Yet somehow he still fumbled three times. In his other three games, he was sacked three times in each contest and was constantly under duress. 2. Establishing the run In 2026, the Raiders have one rushing touchdown; only two players have positive rushing totals and collectively they are averaging 93 yards per game. Despite such abysmal production, they still manage to score 29.5 points per game. Establishing the run keeps the Maye and Patriots offense off the field. It also takes pressure off Kirk Cousins and sets up the play action for big plays in the passing game. 3. Defend the run Not every team has a former Super Bowl MVP at running back. However, the Patriots have a thunder and lightning combination of their own. Rhamondre Stevenson wears down defenses like body shots and leg kicks in the early rounds of an MMA fight. TreyVeyon Henderson is the home-run hitter who is one missed tackle away from running for daylight. Neutralizing them both forces Maye to win the game by himself, something he’s only done once this year. 4. Get wide receivers more involved The Patriots shut down the Bills’ tight end duo of Dalton Kincade and Dawson Knox. The Raiders run more 12/13 personnel (two- and three-tight-end sets) than anyone else in the league. Brock Bowers, specifically, is who they will be keying on. Potentially being without Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis to cover Bowers, the Patriots’ defense is going to have to come up with something ingenious to stop him. Lining up the rest of the Raiders’ pass catchers against practice squad players is a mismatch they must capitalize on. 5. Ball security For two straight weeks, the Raiders’ kick returners have put the football on the ground and given it back to the kicking team. It cost them the division lead against the Chiefs and put them in an 11-point deficit against the New Orleans Saints. This is a trend they can not afford to continue. Especially when it is a one-score game prior to the turnover. It’s quite simple, with better ball security the Raiders are still undefeated.

title: Forcing giveaway-prone Patriots to cough ball up a must for Raiders
summary: A big part of the Las Vegas Raiders 3-1 overall mark after the first four games of the season is the team’s 2-0 performance in away games. In Weeks 2 and 3, the Silver & Black topped both the Los Angeles Chargers (26-14) and New Orleans Saints (35-27), respectively, in impressive outings that showcased complementary […]
full_text: (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images) | Getty Images A big part of the Las Vegas Raiders 3-1 overall mark after the first four games of the season is the team’s 2-0 performance in away games. In Weeks 2 and 3, the Silver & Black topped both the Los Angeles Chargers (26-14) and New Orleans Saints (35-27), respectively, in impressive outings that showcased complementary football from Klint Kubiak’s squad. After a tough loss to AFC West rival Kansas City Chiefs (30-27) this past Sunday within the confines of Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas, the Raiders are again away from home with a Week 5 tilt at the New England Patriots (2-2). Without question, Raider Nation is eager for a Raider rebound against the Pats. “Just focusing on the first quarter of the season, what we’ve done well, what we need to improve on, and knowing that our opponents are working on our weaknesses all the time,” Kubiak responded when asked what’s his message to the team coming off a loss. “So, there’s so many little things on each side of the ball that that we’re keying on, and we’re trying to be very intentional about improving.” New England was quite intentional last Sunday when the team handed the AFC East favorite Buffalo Bills a sobering 29-26 loss. It’s a game where the Patriots churned out 402 yards of total offense and overcame their own turnovers by generating two takeaways to stun the Bills and hand Buffalo its first loss of the 2026 season. And that’s where will start with how the Raiders remain unbeaten on the road: Turnovers. “We push down on the gas harder. He trusts the defense. Coach…we got his back. We gotta do our job.” Raiders LB Nakobe Dean speaks after a 30-27 loss to the Chiefs. 🎥: By @MikeDixon_VST pic.twitter.com/JTDy4YIttU — Vegas Sports Today (@VegasSportsTD) October 5, 2026 The Week 4 loss to the Chiefs was the first game this year where Rob Leonard’s Raiders defense didn’t register a takeaway. Heading into that clash of then AFC West unbeatens, Las Vegas paced the league (and is still the leader) in forcing turnovers with nine total. The high mark so far was four against the Saints (with three coming against the Bolts and two against the Dolphins). The host Patriots are tied for the most giveaways this season at 10 (with the Chargers) and if there’s a team ripe for the pickings, it’s New England. Las Vegas needs to return to either jarring the ball loose or picking it off against a team that seemingly can’t protect the football. With Leonard deploying an attacking and fast defense, the Raiders should be able to accomplish this, especially considering the main culprit for the Patriots turnovers is quarterback Drake Maye. The third-year signal caller has seven interceptions and two fumbles lost through four games which should have middle linebacker Nakobe Dean (team-leading three forced fumbles an 32 total tackles, along with 1.5 sacks), safety Jeremy Chinn (two forced fumbles), edge rusher Malcolm Koonce (two forced fumbles, 2.5 sacks), and rookie cornerback Hezekiah Masses (team-leading three interceptions) and the rest of the Raiders defense champing at the bit to square off with New England’s Josh McDaniels-led offense. “It always comes back to fundamentals and execution, especially in the critical moments. That they felt the reality of what you preach every day, of being locked in, regardless of the environment and how loud it is. A call can’t save you,” Leonard said on the lessons he hopes his defense learned in the loss to Kansas City. “It comes down to fundamentals and taking the ball away and playing blocks the right way, releasing blocks, being on the same page in coverage.” With weather projections indicating a 75 percent chance of heavy rain in Foxborough during Sunday’s game, Las Vegas must be locked in on stopping the Patriots ground game that’s produced 471 yards through four games which ranks them 11th most in the league. Attacking the ball carriers and making the Patriots one dimensional will help the Raiders’ rebound quest. Klint Kubiak just confirmed that Ashton Jeanty is questionable for Sunday’s game against the New England Patriots. He’ll travel with the team and “do his best to go” Rookie Mike Washington Jr. is next man up in the #Raiders backfield, with their lone rushing TD this season. — Levi Edwards (@theleviedwards) October 9, 2026 Flip it to Kubiak’s offense and he needs to rejuvenate a Raiders run game that’s been spinning its wheels as of late. And the late addition of starting running back Ashton Jeanty to the injury report compounds matters. The talented tailback hasn’t looked completely healthy and he didn’t practice on Friday before Las Vegas traveled to New England. Fortunately for Kubiak, he does have talented rookie running back Mike Washington Jr. in tow and the Arkansas product has the team’s lone touchdown run on the year. There’s also veteran running back Dylan Laube on the depth chart and a pair of tailbacks on the practice squad — undrafted rookie Roman Hemby and Owen Wright — if Jeanty can’t go against the Patriots. “I think we just have to pay attention to our details,” Raiders offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko said when asked what it’ll take to get a consistent run game. “Starting with ourselves, what we’re asking of the players, how we’re attacking each plan, what we are attacking each game plan. Then, presenting a great plan to the players, allowing them to be detailed so they can go out, play fast, and attack it. That’s what we’re looking forward to doing.” If the Patriots are able to replicate what opposing defenses have done — stacking the box against the Raiders heavy formations and stifling the run — Kubiak’s passing attack led by super veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins and tight end (apparently in name only now) Brock Bowers needs to be on point. Especially if inclement weather if it does pour. This is where it’s compounding matters for both Las Vegas and New England, however. The Raiders will be without normal starting wide receiver Jalen Nailor (concussion) while the Patriots will be without its top two cornerbacks Christian Gonzalez (shoulder) and Carlton Davis (neck) and a third Channing Canada (hamstring). Expect Cousins to look frequently at Bowers and rising wide receiver Cody White when the attack goes aerial. And against an ailing secondary, success should be plentiful. Quotes of Note “Everything we do starts in practice, and as we practice, we build confidence with guys, and when opportunities come by, taking advantage of those opportunities. I think that a lot of those times, as long as guys keep their head down, they work, those things happen organically. So, when you see a guy’s number called, he makes a play, and then that always gets more playing time.” —Las Vegas Raiders offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko on what rookie wide receiver Malik Benson needs to do to get more playing time/opportunities on offense “Yeah, I mean I would tell you candidly, but I’m not going to. But I mean, we’re going to go down being aggressive, whatever that means. That’s all I’ll say about that.” —Las Vegas Raiders defensive coordinator Rob Leonard when asked where the team has to improve when deploying Cover Zero looks.

title: Raiders Mailbag: What’s going on with offensive line?
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders hit the road in Week 5 to take on the New England Patriots in an early-season battle that could have big playoff implications down the line. So, we’ll be touching on the upcoming game and focusing heavily on the Raiders’ offensive line for this week’s mailbag. Let’s get to it! Q: […]
full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders hit the road in Week 5 to take on the New England Patriots in an early-season battle that could have big playoff implications down the line. So, we’ll be touching on the upcoming game and focusing heavily on the Raiders’ offensive line for this week’s mailbag. Let’s get to it! Q: Did Jackson Powers-Johnson get locked into the starting guard position after missing the Kansas City game and seeing Chris Jones dominate? A: I wouldn’t go as far as saying Powers-Johnson is “locked into” the starting spot because he’s been so hit or miss this season, and his entire career, really. But Caleb Rogers certainly blew an opportunity to unseat JPJ with how much Rogers struggled against Jones. Of course, that’s a future Hall of Famer who has made guards much better than Rogers look bad on plenty of occasions. So, it’s understandable that the second-year pro had a rough game, but at least to me, nothing about his performance said that a lineup change needs to be made. In other words, I think it’s still a fluid situation where Powers-Johnson shouldn’t feel too comfortable as a starter. However, I’m expecting him to be with the first-string offense in New England. Q: With the amount of free agent money and draft capital the Raiders spent on the O-line these last two offseasons, do you think it’s expected they will have, at least, a top-15 pass-blocking and run-blocking line by the end of this season? A: Well, part of the problem is that the draft capital they’ve used on the offensive line isn’t seeing the field much right now. Rogers played last week because the guy in front of him was injured, Trey Zuhn III is the swing tackle/jumbo tight end who has played just nine snaps this season, and Charles Grant has only gotten a significant amount of playing time in one game (Week 18 versus the Chiefs last year). In free agency, Tyler Linderbaum got a massive contract, but Spencer Burford is only making about $3.3 million . So, outside of Linderbaum, the Raiders are getting little to nothing from their significant investments in the offensive line over the last two offseasons. That’s an area of improvement for John Spytek moving forward because his third-round picks (Rogers, Grant, Zuhn, Darien Porter and Keyron Crawford) are looking pretty rough right now. Of course, those guys can contribute down the line, but the immediate return is low. But to answer your question, I do think getting back to an average offensive line is a reasonable expectation. I’d say the unit is falling short of that right now, but they have the potential to get there by the end of the season. Otherwise, some significant changes will need to be made moving forward. Q: Thanks for breaking down Rob Leonard’s “MEG” coverage last week! Can you do a similar explanation of Kubiak’s offensive line scheme and how that scheme fits or doesn’t fit our main starters and key backups (i.e. Rogers, Zuhn, Grant)? Does this fit with the offensive lines Rick Dennison has coached? I know the Raiders run a lot of wide-zone, but I don’t have much understanding of how that differs from power, duo, or any other system, nor how well our line is doing at adapting to Kubiak’s playbook, in your opinion? A: On Dennison, he’s been coaching with the Kubiaks for decades, breaking into coaching under Gary Kubiak (Klint’s dad) with the Denver Broncos in 1995. Gary was the Broncos’ offensive coordinator at the time, while Mike Shanahan was the head coach. So, Dennison definitely knows how to coach offensive linemen in this offense. What differs between a wide-zone rushing attack versus a gap/power scheme is that the entire offensive line is moving together and in the same direction as the running back, while the latter includes more down blocks and a puller or two unless it’s duo. So, in gap runs, three or four offensive linemen are going the opposite direction of the running back, with one or two pullers lead blocking or moving in the same direction as the running back. Duo is a little different because there is no puller, so all five offensive linemen (and the tight end) down block or have a double team, and in the opposite direction of the back. The other big difference in the two schemes is that the running back has more flexibility to bounce or cutback in zone, whereas gap runs are more strict about where to hit the hole. In zone, a running back will have a targeted area initially, but he’s taught to adjust based on the defense to make the defense wrong. It’s a similar process with the line, where they can be more patient and ride the defender they’re blocking where he wants to go and exaggerate the movement. For example, if an offensive tackle is blocking a defensive end that pinches or slants inside, the tackle will try to push the defensive end all the way inside and into the center. But in a gap scheme, the goal is to run into a specific gap and only bounce outside if it’s absolutely necessary (i.e., someone losing up front), so that tackle would try to cut off the end and wall him off to keep the B-gap open if that’s where the play is designed to hit. As a result, a gap-heavy team is going to want bigger but less athletic offensive linemen who can move 300-pound defensive tackles out of the way. Whereas a zone-heavy team is willing to sacrifice size and strength for linemen who can move and adjust based on the defense. Don’t get me wrong, linemen still need plenty of strength and athleticism in either system. But how much importance a team places on strength versus athleticism varies based on the scheme. When it comes to the Raiders, they have a lot of linemen who fit the wide zone scheme. That’s where Kolton Miller is at his best in the running game, Linderbaum is really athletic, as are Zuhn and Rogers. Grant didn’t test well at the combine, but his quickness and agility stood out on tape to execute reach blocks and fit into a wide zone system. JPJ is probably a better fit in a gap scheme, but he was plenty athletic at Oregon to execute zone blocks. His issues are more mental because he keeps going for the kill shot instead of recognizing when he just needs to get in front of or get a hat on a defender. And a big reason why Burford is even on the team is that he played in the Kubiak/Shanahan scheme with the 49ers. I didn’t think DJ Glaze would be a good fit with Kubiak at tackle because he isn’t very athletic. But Glaze is proving me wrong and playing really well right now. So, I think the Raiders have the right (or enough) pieces to put it all together. But a zone scheme does require more continuity since the entire line is moving together (it’s kind of similar to pass protection in that regard), and that can take some time to build. Hopefully, we start seeing some improvements in the coming weeks now that the line has a few games together under its belt. Q: How do you feel about the starting OTs right now? Kolton Miller looking kinda older? Is he declining slightly? I’ve heard that Glaze is benefiting from chips and scheme help, then I’ve heard that he’s much improved regardless of any help. Where do you stand on Glaze? A: Someone else asked if Glaze is playing well enough at right tackle that it makes sense to give Zuhn reps at guard instead of tackle . Miller definitely had a bad game last week, one of the worst I’ve seen from him in a while. But he was pretty good during the first three weeks, to the point where I’m not worried about the left tackle spot right now. But he turned 31 on Friday (happy birthday, Kolton!), so it certainly wouldn’t be a bad idea to add a contingency plan on the blind side this offseason. Could that be Grant’s job in the future? Maybe, but we’ve barely seen him play and, barring an injury, it doesn’t seem like that will change anytime soon. I’m not saying this would happen, but even if the Raiders decide to move on from Miller in the spring, I think they’d still have to bring in some competition for Grant rather…

title: What’s wrong with Drake Maye ahead of New England Patriots-Las Vegas Raiders Week 5 game?
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders are looking to bounce back and stay firmly in the AFC Playoff conversation during their Week 5 matchup against the New England Patriots. To preview the contest, Silver and Black Pride reached out to our friends at Pats Pulpit, and Taylor Kyles was kind enough to answer a few questions about […]
full_text: (Photo by Rich Storry/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders are looking to bounce back and stay firmly in the AFC Playoff conversation during their Week 5 matchup against the New England Patriots . To preview the contest, Silver and Black Pride reached out to our friends at Pats Pulpit, and Taylor Kyles was kind enough to answer a few questions about the Patriots for Raider Nation. Q: Drake Maye was an MVP candidate last year and looked anything but that during the first three weeks of the season. What’s been the difference between his play in the last two years? Is there a sense that Maye has turned the corner after having his first good performance in Week 4? A: Drake Maye’s arm talent, athleticism, and instincts were evident during his rookie season, but he was held back by a lackluster supporting cast, a basic scheme, and poor leadership. Under HC Mike Vrabel and OC Josh McDaniels, Maye’s potential was on full display thanks to a proven system, an upgraded, if less-than-stellar supporting cast, and a more experienced coaching staff. His fundamentals and willingness to climb the pocket or keep his eyes downfield when scrambling took massive steps forward, though fumbles and down-to-down consistency were still work in progress. Through the first three weeks of this season, Maye’s ball security, footwork, and understanding of when to take chances all took significant steps back, leading to several moments that had people questioning if he was the same guy. The ability was still there, and overall Maye was making more positive plays than negative, but too much of the bad was inexcusable, and it kept putting the team in bad positions. Maye didn’t exactly nip his turnover problem in the bud last week, but he looked far more like 2025 Maye by making crucial plays with his legs and delivering several accurate and well-timed throws downfield. The hope is Maye continues trending in that direction, but he has to prove that on the field. Q: Along similar lines, a lot was made about Will Campbell’s arm length and the Patriots’ ability to protect Maye after the Super Bowl. How has the offensive line looked so far in 2026? How well do they handle stunts, simulated pressures, creeper blitzes, etc., which the Raiders have learned heavily on through the first four weeks? A: The Patriots have surrendered pressure at a pretty high rate, but pass protection has done a solid job keeping Maye upright overall. LT Will Campbell, LG Alijah Vera-Tucker, and C Jared Wilson are still learning to work together consistently against stunts. Vera-Tucker and Wilson have been impressive overall. Campbell has sneakily struggled against top-notch edge rushers one-on-one this season, and that was exposed last week when he was left on an island against Greg Rousseau. If I were the Raiders, I’d have Maxx Crosby challenge Campbell on money downs and some obvious passing situations. RG Mike Onwenu going down was a huge hit, as he’s arguably the team’s best offensive lineman. He’s been replaced by usual C/LG Ben Brown, who gave up a few pressures but competed well against a tough Buffalo interior. RT Morgan Moses is currently the team’s best lineman, but his explosiveness and mobility have been limited by a foot injury. He’s survived on patience, technique, and his natural talent, but he’ll likely need chip help against Vegas’ explosive edge rushers. Schematically, New England has done well to identify and stop most simulated pressures and blitzes, thanks in large part to Rhamondre Stevenson being one of the league’s best pass-protecting backs. The offense has struggled against blitzes, but that’s had more to do with the creation of one-on-one matchups and increased ability to create confusion with stunts. Q: One of New England’s biggest offseason additions, wide receiver A.J. Brown, is currently on injured reserve and won’t be playing on Sunday. Who has picked up the slack? Is there a pass-catcher you think can have a big impact against the Raiders? A: Romeo Doubs has improved each week since catching zero passes in his debut. Last week, the chemistry he and Maye showed on vertical routes this summer was on full display, including back-to-back plays where Doubs caught a hole shot before scoring on a backside post. Maye loves his X receivers, and though Doubs doesn’t fit the prototypical mold, he’s big and experienced enough to win one-on-one, particularly in the red zone. I’d expect Maye to target him early and often against a young Raiders cornerback group, especially with Mack Hollins missing this week’s game. Q: Despite the offense’s struggles to begin the campaign, the Patriots’ defense has been stingy, ranking sixth in points and yards allowed. If you’re Klint Kubiak, how would you go about attacking this defense? Conversely, what would you say to avoid doing? A: I would attack the Patriots’ interior defensive line in the ground game first and foremost. The group looked much better last week than they had the previous three, which was impressive with Christian Barmore out, but that inconsistency must be tested. Specifically, I’d use zone runs that get the play flowing one way before cutting back behind potential overflow. In the passing game, I’d literally target Brock Bowers 15-20 times. With Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis out for this game, Bowers will have a size advantage over all of New England’s corners and a talent advantage over everyone but maybe Marcus Jones. Force the Patriots to do everything in their power to take Bowers away, then see if you can catch them sleeping elsewhere. Q: Similar to the wide receivers, edge defender Harold Landry III hasn’t played yet this season. Who has filled in for Landry? Is there another defensive lineman who you think will make an impact against the Raiders? A: Dre’Mont Jones has stepped up as the veteran in the room, and he’s exceeded most people’s expectations despite being limited a bit by injury. He’s currently top-10 among edge rushers in pass rush win rate and pressure rate, and it shows on the tape with his advanced hand-fighting and instincts. That said, Elijah Ponder and Gabe Jacas have come on strong to round out the group. Ponder went from an undrafted rookie role player to a starter this season, and he’s blooming into the quick winner he showed the potential to be at Cal Poly. Jacas missed the entire spring due to a contract dispute and had a slightly late start to the summer, but his improvement has been steady since, and he’s become one of the defense’s top playmakers. Ponder and Jacas are still pretty raw, but they’re tough, heads-up players with bright futures.

full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - SEPTEMBER 29: Ja'Marr Chase #1 of the Cincinnati Bengals runs with the ball while being chased by Keion Crossen #27 of the Miami Dolphins in the fourth quarter at Paycor Stadium on September 29, 2022 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Dylan Buell/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Miami Dolphins host the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 5, looking to pull off the upset for their first win of the year. Early in the week, it appeared the Bengals may come into Sunday’s game without their top two receivers as Ja’Marr Chase worked his way through the concussion protocol and Tee Higgins dealt with groin and neck issues. On Sunday, both players were cleared to play, avoiding the inactive players list for Cincinnati. The Bengals will be without safety Kyle Duggar, who was ruled out with a quadriceps injury. He led Cincinnati’s inactive list, which also included center Connor Lew, tackle Myles Hinton, tight end Jack Endries, wide receiver Colbie Young, and defensive tackle Landon Robinson. The Dolphins ruled four players out of the game on Friday’s injury report (not including cornerback Storm Duck, who is practicing but has not been activated from the physically unable to perform list): edge rusher Robert Beal, Jr. (hamstring), wide receiver Caleb Douglas (ankle), tight end Justin Joly (concussion), and cornerback Reese Taylor (quadriceps). Miami’s inactive list started with those four. Along with the injured players, Miami also listed running back Kaytron Allen, guard DJ Campbell, and tackle Chukwuebuka Godrick as inactive. Allen was claimed off waivers this week from the Washington Commanders and likely needs more time to get up to speed on the playbook. The Dolphins elevated running back Carlos Washington from the practice squad to provide depth behind Jaylen Wright and Ollie Gordon II.

summary: The Miami Dolphins have started the 2026 season 0-4, but that does not mean the fans do not trust that the team is headed in the right direction. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Miami Dolphins have started the 2026 season 0-4, but that does not mean the fans do not trust that the team is headed in the right direction. Despite the Week 4 loss to the Minnesota Vikings, the team showed growth and development, which are key parts of a rebuild for the league’s youngest roster. The fans seem to appreciate those signs of improvement. Heading into Week 5, the Dolphins will face a struggling Cincinnati Bengals team. After a 2-0 start to the year, they have dropped their last two contests to fall to 2-2 and now sit last in the AFC North. Cincinnati will come into this game looking to take advantage of a winless Dolphins team and right the ship. Miami should expect the Bengals to throw everything they have at this game. Can Miami do enough to pull off the Week 5 upset as they head into their bye week in Week 6? According to the oddsmakers at FanDuel Sportsbook , the Bengals are seven-point favorites for today’s game. Dolphins fan confidence A 0-4 start to the season typically tanks the fan trust in a team. For example, the SB Nation Reacts fan confidence survey for the Los Angeles Chargers this week came back with just six percent of their fans trusting in the direction of the team. Beginning the year with four-straight losses is typically time for the fan base to panic. Not when it comes to the Dolphins in 2026. Miami is expected to struggle this year. They tore the team down to the bare bones during the offseason and have started rebuilding, but it will likely take more than one offseason. The positives this year are the experience a team built primarily around rookie and second-year players can gain and the growth they can show. They are doing exactly that, and the fan confidence continues to grow with them. Last week, 79 percent of responses said fans trust the team, just one percent below our season high. This week, we blew past that mark. Miami may be 0-4, but 87 percent of the fans seem to think the team is headed in the right direction. title: Miami Dolphins offensive line review: Tracking the guards in Week 4
summary: The Miami Dolphins fell to the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, dropping to 0-4 as they continue navigating a significant roster rebuild. That is especially true along the offensive line, where rookie left guard Kadyn Proctor and […]
full_text: The Miami Dolphins fell to the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, dropping to 0-4 as they continue navigating a significant roster rebuild. While wins and losses matter, much of the focus in 2026 remains on the development of Miami’s young talent. That is especially true along the offensive line, where rookie left guard Kadyn Proctor and second-year right guard Jonah Savaiinaea are important pieces of the team’s future. How are they performing this season? Each week, we take a closer look at the guards and what is being said about their most recent performance. Kadyn Proctor Game Snap Counts Penalties PFF Overall Grade PFF Run Blocking PFF Pass Protection 9/13, @ Raiders 59 (100%) 1 71.2 79.0 63.4 9/20, @ 49ers 56 (100%) 2 62.0 72.4 39.1 9/27, vs. Chiefs 73 (100%) 0 57.5 51.1 71.3 10/4, @ Vikings 39 (100%) 0 51.2 48.6 64.9 Jonah Savaiinaea Game Snap Counts Penalties PFF Overall Grade PFF Run Blocking PFF Pass Protection 9/13, @ Raiders 59 (100%) 0 47.6 50.9 38.2 9/20, @ 49ers 56 (100%) 0 65.9 68.5 46.1 9/27, vs. Chiefs 73 (100%) 0 56.6 58.4 47.5 10/4, @ Vikings 39 (100%) 0 49.5 44.6 77.5 What We Learned First: 39 snaps?! Keep the alarmingly small sample size in mind when looking at the grading. Also, we knew this was going to be a tough game against an aggressive defense. The Dolphins’ ascending left tackle Patrick Paul had two holding penalties plus a third one that was declined. We’ve talked before about the, well, subjective nature of PFF grading . I don’t put a lot of stock in the grades themselves as much as the trends. Is Kadyn Proctor’s run blocking experiencing a decline? Is Jonah Savaiinaea improving as a pass blocker? Where will these two be grading at the end of the year compared to where they started? For more context, I thought I would poke around the intertubes and see what others had to say: On October 6, Kyle Crabbs of LockedOn Dolphins and AtoZSports completed his “first-quarter report.” He gives Kadyn Proctor a B and said he is a player who “moves the needle.” Also on October 6, Barry Jackson with the Miami Herald posted a story on Jonah Savaiinaea, commenting that Savaiinaea hasn’t given up a sack yet and is a “clearly better player than he was a year ago.” On October 4, Alain Poupart of Sports Illustrated said in a mailbag that “there is no question that Savaiinaea has looked better early in his second season than he did as a rookie,” and, despite some work to do in pass protection, “he has looked good in the running game and there has been a clear improvement.” In his review of the offensive line play against the Vikings , offensive line coach Eric Smith graded both players lower than in previous weeks. Smith remains bullish on Proctor’s long-term outlook, saying the rookie’s physical tools are obvious and that “we’re going to have a really good player here.” His concerns centered more on communication, processing and run-game execution than physical limitations. As for Savaiinaea, Smith called it his lowest-graded game of the season but said his Year 2 improvement is real and expects him to bounce back in the coming weeks. Four games into the season, the trend line remains encouraging. Proctor continues to earn praise for his upside, while Savaiinaea is drawing recognition for tangible improvement from a difficult rookie season. Let’s see how they do against the Bengals on Sunday. The tracker will be updated each week throughout the season. For a more in-depth breakdown of Proctor’s and Savaiinaea’s performance, check out offensive line Coach Eric Smith’s film analysis of the game, which you can find on his YouTube channel, Focused on Fins .
